地下, of Party organization operating in secret. The word is used throughout for what the Juntong was hunting, and the chapter's structure follows the hunt: find the cell, take one member, turn him, use him to identify the rest.

The concession police forces employed Chinese detectives under foreign command, and the Juntong placed its own men among them. That is how, in the following chapter, poison reaches a prisoner in French custody. The arrangement is the practical answer to the jurisdictional problem the concessions posed.

The Shanghai Municipal Police in the International Settlement and the French concession police were separate forces answerable to their own authorities. Prisoners taken by them could be handed over to the Chinese side, and the negotiation of those handovers runs through the chapter.

Juntong men habitually operated under assumed names, and Shen Zui records several of his own colleagues by both. The book's habit of giving alias and real name together is a small mark of its documentary intent.

眼线, literally an 'eye-line'. The distinction between an informer, a bought contact and an enrolled operative matters throughout: the Juntong ran far more of the first two than the third, and Shen Zui gives the ratios in the Chungking chapter.

Cash rewards for cases broken were a standing feature of the service and, as the Chungking chapter shows at length, a standing source of its corruption. Here they appear as the incentive behind arrests made on thin evidence.
口供. The word covers both a statement and what was extracted under torture, and the chapter uses it for both without distinction, as the organization did.

The disposal method described more than once: the victim knocked senseless or killed, put into a sack and dropped into the Whangpoo. Shen Zui gives it in the same enumerative register as the organizational detail around it.

The tortures section catalogues methods rather than describing individual cases, which is how such material reached print in the 文史资料 series: institutional description was publishable where a named victim often was not.

Among the implements listed. The chapter names materials and methods but very few of the people they were used on, and the asymmetry is worth noticing: Shen Zui is far more specific about his colleagues than about their prisoners.

The Juntong's special training classes, the subject of chapter 1. Shen Zui taught operational technique at many of them and edited the lecture notes, and this chapter's cases became teaching material there.

特训班. The Shanghai cases were written up as case studies for these classes, which is Shen Zui's warrant for the detail he gives: he is drawing on material he compiled and taught rather than on recollection alone.
Photographic files were central to the surveillance system, and the Chungking chapter describes a studio run at a loss to feed them. Here the concern is identification of suspects in the street.

Sun Yat-sen (1866-1925), founder of the Republic. His widow Song Qingling's standing derived from him, and it is precisely that standing which, as Shen Zui explains, made her untouchable and made those around her targets instead.
Japanese pressure on Shanghai runs beneath this whole chapter: the fighting of 1932, the position of Hongkou, and the approach of the full war in 1937 which ends the period it covers.

The Old Cha station and others appear as the point where a street arrest became a formal one. The chapter's arrests divide sharply into the open kind, processed through a station, and the secret kind, which left no record at all.

The Party's underground was organized so that members knew only their own small group. The Juntong's method, as this chapter sets it out, was to break one member and work outward, which is why a single defection like Lu Haifang's was worth so much to them.
联络. The chapter is unusually specific about how contact was maintained and how it was broken, because that was the operational knowledge Shen Zui taught.
Domestic detail of this kind is rare in the book and tends to appear where Shen Zui is describing his own circumstances rather than the organization's work.

The Shanghai press is both a subject of this chapter and a source for it: what appeared in the papers about the killings, and what did not, is one of the few external checks available on Shen Zui's account.
行动组, the arm that carried out arrests, kidnappings and killings. Zhao Lijun's Shanghai operations group is the unit responsible for most of what this chapter describes.

The event stands behind half this book and gets its full treatment in the chapter on Zhang Xueliang's detention. In December 1936 Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng arrested Chiang Kai-shek at Xi'an to force an end to the civil war against the Communists and a united resistance to Japan; Chiang was released within the fortnight after negotiations in which Zhou Enlai took part, and the Nationalist-Communist united front followed. Zhang, who flew back to Nanking with his captive, spent the rest of Chiang's life in custody for it.

ch05.note: 第二次反共高潮. In January 1941 Nationalist forces destroyed the New Fourth Army headquarters in southern Anhwei, killing or capturing most of its personnel. Known as the New Fourth Army Incident or the Wannan Incident, it effectively ended the united front as a working arrangement. Ye Ting was captured; his deputy Xiang Ying was killed. The outline Shen Zui gives, seven divisions under Gu Zhutong, matches the standard account.
Gu Zhutong (1893-1987), commander-in-chief of the Third War Zone and the officer who directed the operation against the New Fourth Army. He went to Taiwan in 1949.

Ye Ting (1896-1946), a founder of the Chinese Communist Party's military tradition, commander of the New Fourth Army, held from January 1941 until March 1946. He died weeks after his release when the aircraft carrying him crashed near Yenan. Shen Zui had personal charge of arrangements for his custody in Chungking, which is the warrant for this chapter.
七星岩, the celebrated cave system at Kweilin. Ye Ting was held in a cave near it, with Juntong operatives inside and military police outside.
上饶 in Kiangsi, seat of the Third War Zone headquarters and site of the concentration camp where New Fourth Army personnel taken in the incident were held.

Shen Zui's brother, head of the Juntong's Kweilin operations group and the officer responsible for guarding Ye Ting. A second brother, Shen Yulong, appears in the Chungking chapter as head of an arsenal guard group. The family's penetration of the service is not remarked on by the author.
Commander of the Juntong's operatives' regiment, the unit that furnished the warders for the Juntong's prisons and, as the Chungking chapter records, carried out its killings.

The lamp is the chapter's organizing image. Ye Ting carries it off the aircraft, keeps it through three years of confinement, and takes it down from the wall on the day of his release. Shen Zui, who reports it twice without drawing a conclusion, is a better witness here than he is elsewhere in the book.

ch05.anchor: I will certainly not trim my hair and beard in order to see anyone I have no wish to see.
ch05.note: The refusal to cut his hair is the chapter's second image and the one Shen Zui says he remembers most exactly. Its logic is stated plainly by the prisoner: an officer who has done no wrong, held without cause, will not make himself presentable for his captors. Shen Zui was sent to get the hair cut because Chiang Kai-shek might want to see him; the errand and its failure are reported in the same flat register.

Chen Cheng (1898-1965), commander-in-chief of the Sixth War Zone and one of Chiang Kai-shek's most senior generals, later premier and vice-president on Taiwan. His two attempts to recruit Ye Ting as his own deputy, and his going in with his head high and coming out crestfallen, are Shen Zui's account and are not independently documented.

白公馆, built as the Xiangshan villa by the Szechwan warlord Bai Ju and taken over as a Juntong prison. With Zhazidong, inside the same SACO compound, it became after 1949 the best-known site of Nationalist political imprisonment in China; both are now museums.
渣滓洞, a disused coal pit inside the SACO compound converted into a prison. Most of those held there were killed in the days before the Communist entry into Chungking in November 1949.

禁地. Shen Zui's term for the area of SACO reserved for senior political prisoners, closed even to ordinary Juntong operatives. Ye Ting and Liao Chengzhi were held within it in separate single-storey buildings.

Superintendent of the Baigongguan detention house. Shen Zui calls him a savage who beat and cursed prisoners at every turn, and then records that Ye Ting advised him not to go too far with people -- the prisoner counselling the gaoler.

Liao Chengzhi (1908-1983), son of the Nationalist leader Liao Zhongkai, held by the Juntong from 1942 and released in the same March 1946 exchange. Shen Zui personally escorted him to the People's Political Council for the handover.

Ma Fawu (1893-1992), a Nationalist general captured by Communist forces in 1945, exchanged for Ye Ting in March 1946. The exchange is documented; Shen Zui's date of 4 March is consistent with the record.
Shao Lizi (1882-1967), a senior Nationalist figure who acted repeatedly as an intermediary with the Communists and remained on the mainland after 1949.

Ye Xiangzhi, deputy head of the Juntong's Second Department, who escorted Ye Ting to the Eighth Route Army office. He appears in the Chungking chapter as a head of the Yu special district and later became a senior intelligence figure on Taiwan.

ch05.anchor: That is exactly where the Communists are formidable.
ch05.note: Dai Li's closing remark, after a long silence, on being told that the first thing Ye Ting meant to do on release was ask the Party to restore his membership. Shen Zui gives it without comment and ends the chapter there. The whole of his own errand -- to soften the prisoner by comforts and bring him over -- is judged by it.

ch05.anchor: The first thing I shall do when I get out is to ask the Party to restore my membership.
ch05.note: Ye Ting had been separated from the Party since 1927 and was not a member at the time of his capture; his application was approved shortly after his release. Shen Zui's admission that he had never considered this, and understood nothing of what it meant, is the most direct statement of his own former incomprehension in the book so far, and it is doing the work the 1962-66 framing required of him. It is also, on the evidence of the rest of the chapter, probably true.

ch06.note: 劫持统帅. On 31 December 1936 a military tribunal in Nanking, presided over by Li Liejun, tried Zhang for his part in the Xi'an Incident and sentenced him to ten years' imprisonment with five years' deprivation of civil rights. A special pardon followed within days — but it remanded him to the 'strict control' (管束) of the Military Affairs Commission, the legal fiction under which he was then held without any term at all, in the end for more than half a century. Shen's 'ten-year sentence' is the tribunal's; the detention it dressed up had no expiry, which is the fact the rest of this chapter keeps running into. Corroborated.

雪窦寺, a Buddhist temple in the hills above Xikou, Chiang Kai-shek's home town in Fenghua, Zhejiang. Zhang was moved there in January 1937, and the location — under the eaves of Chiang's own native place — is corroborated by every account of the confinement.

Translation uncertainty. The scan prints an OCR-resistant three-character name the machine read as 李和久桢; 李仲桢 (Li Zhongzhen) is the reading adopted, but it could not be confirmed at the available resolution and no outside source for Dai Li's placement of a Xiuwen magistrate has been found. Treat the romanization as provisional.
丈, ten Chinese feet: about 3.3 metres. Ten zhang is on the order of thirty metres.

玄天洞, a Daoist cave-temple north of the Xifeng county town, where General Yang Hucheng was held with his family for most of 1938-1946. His story ends where this book will later take it: murdered with his son and daughter on Chiang Kai-shek's orders in September 1949 at Songlinpo in Chungking — the same hillside where Zhang, in this chapter, is lodged on his way to Taiwan.

三潭印月, the celebrated West Lake sight at Hangzhou: three small stone pagodas standing in the water off Lesser Yingzhou island. An arsenal reproducing it in its cooling reservoir says something about the garden-building instincts of wartime Nationalist institutions even deep in the Guizhou mountains.
亩, the Chinese acre: one-fifteenth of a hectare. A hundred mu is about six and a half hectares, or sixteen English acres.

于凤至 (1897-1990), Zhang's wife from 1916, by an arrangement of his father's. Shen dates her departure for America to 1943; the standard accounts are against him — she left in 1940, for treatment of breast cancer, and never saw Zhang free again. She was divorced from him, by consent and at long distance, in 1964, so that he could marry Zhao Yidi, and died in Los Angeles in 1990. Contradicted on the date; corroborated in everything else.

赵一荻 (1912-2000), Zhao Yidi, daughter of a senior Beiyang railways official, who scandalised her family by joining Zhang in 1929 and then followed him into every one of his prisons. 赵四小姐, 'Fourth Miss Zhao,' was what the whole country called her; the book uses the nickname as naturally as the guards did. She married Zhang in Taiwan in 1964 and outlived the century with him. Corroborated.

许建业. Not to be confused with the Communist labour organiser of exactly the same name, executed in Chungking in 1949, who became the model for Xu Yunfeng in the novel Red Crag. This Xu Jianye is a Juntong officer about whom nothing further is recorded; the coincidence of names is complete.

老帅: Zhang Zuolin, the Fengtian warlord who ruled Manchuria until the Japanese Kwantung Army blew up his train at Huanggutun outside Mukden in June 1928. 少帅, the Young Marshal, was and has remained his son's universal sobriquet — used here, tellingly, by the family servants a decade and a half after there was any army left to be marshal of.

莫德惠 (1883-1968), a senior Manchurian statesman who had negotiated with Moscow over the Chinese Eastern Railway in 1929 and sat on the People's Political Council through the war. That he was one of the only outsiders permitted to visit Zhang is corroborated by many accounts, including Zhang's own later oral history; he followed the government to Taiwan and headed the Examination Yuan in the 1950s.

ch06.anchor: There is a poem to prove it.
ch06.note: The poem is Ma Junwu's 哀沈阳 ('Lament for Shenyang', 1931): 赵四风流朱五狂，翩翩蝴蝶正当行… — 'Fourth Miss Zhao is amorous, Fifth Miss Zhu is wild, and the fluttering Butterfly is all the rage… who cares that the eastern army has entered Shenyang?' It fixed in the public mind forever the image of Zhang dancing with the film star Hu Die while Manchuria fell. Historians treat it as pure slander: Hu Die was travelling to Peiping with a Mingxing film crew when Mukden fell, and denied to the end of her life ever having met Zhang at all. Note that even Zhang's denial as Shen reports it — one dance, nothing more — concedes more than the record supports; the poem's fiction was durable enough to work on the secret police themselves.

胡蝶 (1908-1989), 'Butterfly Wu' in the period English press, the reigning star of Chinese cinema through the 1930s. What Shen declines to explain is why she is at Dai Li's private table: from about 1943 until Dai's death she was kept by him in Chungking as his mistress, an arrangement documented in Frederic Wakeman's Spymaster and remembered at length elsewhere in Shen's own writings. The scene's easy domesticity — lunch for three, Dai stepping out to the telephone — is the liaison in plain sight.

ch06.anchor: the concentrated study of Ming history
ch06.note: Corroborated. Zhang's Ming-history project in captivity is well documented — Chiang Kai-shek himself had directed him toward the Ming and toward Wang Yangming as edifying reading, which gives the hobby the same flavour as the geography of his prisons (see the Yangming Cave note). In Taiwan he eventually abandoned the Ming for New Testament theology.

夜郎国. Yelang was the small kingdom of Han-dynasty Guizhou whose ruler famously asked the Han envoy whether Han or Yelang was the greater; 夜郎自大, 'Yelang thinks itself big,' has been proverbial for provincial self-importance ever since. Zhang's joke lands two ways at once: Guizhou as the middle of nowhere, and a prisoner measuring how far from the world he has been put.

阳明洞. The cave is named for Wang Yangming (王守仁, 1472-1529), the Ming philosopher-statesman banished in 1508 to the Longchang post station in what is now Xiuwen, where — in this cave — he had the enlightenment that founded his school. Zhang was thus imprisoned inside the metaphor: the exiled statesman who is to purify his mind and leave politics alone. Shen spells the programme out below, and it did not stop at the mainland — see the note on Caoshan.

Uncorroborated, and Shen says as much (外间流传, word going round outside). The watch-as-hint story circulates in several incompatible versions: popular tellings attach it to Chiang's seventieth birthday in 1956, with Chiang answering the hint by return gift — a 1936 calendar and embroidered slippers in one version, a cane or a fishing rod in others — and a separate 1945 story has Mo Dehui delivering a pocket watch from Chiang to Zhang. The 'centenary' model is itself a difficulty: Omega's centenary fell in 1948, after the moment this rumour describes. Best read as the folklore of a public that kept count of the ten years even if Chiang did not.

松林坡, a hillside inside the SACO/Ciqikou perimeter at Chungking, where Dai Li built himself the villa Shen describes. It acquired a darker association than anything in this chapter: in September 1949 Yang Hucheng and his children were murdered there, at the Dai Li memorial hall on the same slope, on Chiang Kai-shek's orders — the killing Shen refers to at this chapter's end.

徐远举 (1914-1973), then head of the Second Department of the Chungking Pacification Headquarters and later the Bureau of Secrets Preservation's regional chief in the southwest, in which capacity he directed the prison massacres of November 1949. He is the original of Xu Pengfei, the secret-police villain of the novel Red Crag. Captured in 1949, he died in custody in 1973. Here he is merely a card partner; the reader is meant to feel the ordinariness.

草山, 'Grass Mountain,' the volcanic hot-spring country above Taipei where Zhang was installed from the end of 1946. In 1950 Chiang Kai-shek renamed it Yangmingshan, after Wang Yangming — carrying to Taiwan, and stamping on the map, exactly the programme Shen has just described: first the Yangming Cave of Xiuwen, then the Yangming Cave of Xingguo, then a whole Yangming mountain. The renaming, which stands today, is corroborated; it happened too late for this book's narrative and Shen does not mention it.

Outside accounts, including standard Chinese reference sources, put Liu Yiguang in the FOURTH Whampoa class, not the sixth; Shen — himself no Whampoa man — appears to misremember. The rest is corroborated: Liu remained Zhang's warden for a quarter of a century, eating at his table and sleeping under his roof until he was finally transferred in Taiwan in 1962, and Zhang later called him, in one breath, his benefactor and his enemy.

The February 28 Incident: the island-wide rising against Chen Yi's provincial administration, put down by Nationalist troops with killings whose estimates run from the thousands into the tens of thousands, and the founding trauma of modern Taiwanese politics. Shen's claim that standing orders existed to shoot Zhang rather than let him be freed is consistent with other Juntong participants' memoirs of the Taiwan arrangements, though no documentary order has surfaced; his detail that Chiang positively hoped for a pretext is Shen's inference from inside the service, and should be read as such.

高山族, 'high-mountain people,' the blanket mainland term for Taiwan's indigenous peoples. The February rising was overwhelmingly a movement of Han Taiwanese, and no indigenous assault on the Caoshan district is recorded; the expectation Shen reports says more about how the mainland security men imagined the island than about who was actually in revolt.

Loosely put, and worth untangling since it explains the title 副座. Zhang's 'vice' posts were real and enormous: Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Republic's land, sea and air forces from 1930 — for a time the second soldier of China — and deputy commander of the Bandit Suppression Headquarters for Hubei, Henan and Anhui from 1932. He was never vice-chairman of the Military Affairs Commission as Shen's phrasing suggests; the guards' habit of address had simply outlived the org charts by a decade, which is exactly what finally made Zhang snap at it.

ch07.note: In June 1937 Yang was stripped of his command of the Northwest pacification forces and packed off to Europe and America on an official 'inspection of military affairs' — the standard face-saving exile. The chronology of this paragraph is corroborated throughout: he sailed in June 1937, cut the tour short when the war broke out, and reached Hong Kong at the end of November.

谢葆贞 as this book prints it; standard sources write 谢葆真 (1913-1947). She had joined the Communist Party in 1928, during Yang's command at Anyang, and married him the same year — which is what stands behind the Juntong's judgment, below, that her thinking was 'progressive.' Her death in Chungking in early 1947 is corroborated; accounts of its immediate cause vary, and Shen's version (illness, deliberate neglect and goading) is among the gentler ones.
The Battle of Shanghai, which opened on 13 August 1937 and is dated in Chinese by that formula, as the war's start is dated by July 7th.

李家杰, the first captain of Yang's guard. Shen's portrait of him — the Yunnanese money-hunger, the four hundred dollars, the promotion earned by informing on his prisoners — is this book's own contribution; outside sources add that in July 1946 Li directed the killing of the Communist prisoners Luo Shiwen and Che Yaoxian at Songlinpo, the two men named a few paragraphs below.

熊式辉 (1893-1974), then chairman of Jiangxi province, whose capital was Nanchang; after the war he headed the Nationalist headquarters for the Northeast. Baihuazhou, 'Hundred Flowers Isle,' is the islet park in Nanchang's East Lake.

罗世文 (1904-1946), secretary of the Communist Party's Sichuan provincial committee, and 车耀先 (1894-1946), Chengdu restaurateur, publisher and Party worker, arrested together in 1940. Both were held at Xifeng and both were shot at Songlinpo on 18 August 1946, on Chiang Kai-shek's order — under the direction of Li Jiajie, the same officer who opens this chapter. Corroborated; both are canonical martyrs of the Red Crag literature.

ch07.anchor: Zhang Weilin, Zhang Luping, Feng Chuanqing and Yang Guang
ch07.note: Four of the seven of the 'radio station case': Zhang Luping (张露萍, 1921-1945), a Communist sent into the Juntong's own radio service in 1939, ran a cell inside Dai Li's communications apparatus — Zhang Weilin and Feng Chuanqing were its members — until it was broken in 1940. All were held at Xifeng and executed there in July 1945. That Shen lists them simply as prisoners, without mentioning that they had penetrated his own service, is worth noticing; the fuller story was published only after his book was written.

马寅初 (1882-1982), the economist, jailed 1940-1942 for lecturing against the bureaucratic capital of the four great families; held first at Xifeng, later under house arrest. After 1949 he became president of Peking University, where his 'New Population Theory' and its persecution made him famous a second time. Corroborated.

黄显声 (1896-1949), Manchurian general, organizer of the Northeast volunteer resistance after 1931, arrested 1938. He was held at Xifeng and then Baigongguan, and was shot on 27 November 1949 in the massacre this book keeps returning to. Corroborated.
里, the Chinese mile: half a kilometre. A dozen li is six kilometres or so.

法币, 'legal tender,' the Nationalist currency introduced in 1935. Its wartime and post-war collapse — the inflation Shen keeps returning to — destroyed salaries and savings alike and is one of the standard explanations of the regime's loss of the cities.

万有文库, the Commercial Press's 'Universal Library': a graded reprint series of some four thousand titles, sold by the set as an instant library — exactly what a man would order for a child forbidden to attend school.

李虎臣 (1889-1954). In 1926 Yang Hucheng and Li Huchen held the walled city of Xi'an for eight months against the siege of Liu Zhenhua's Zhensong army, at the cost of tens of thousands of civilian dead by starvation. 'The two tigers holding Chang'an' (二虎守长安) — both men carried 虎 in their names — made Yang's reputation. Corroborated. The scan's OCR gave the name as 李虎城; the reading 李虎臣 is certain from the history.

龚国彦. The scan is badly degraded wherever this name occurs — the OCR produced ten different misreadings of it — but the printed form is clearly 龚 (crop-verified), and the man appears under this name in other accounts of Yang's imprisonment.

周养浩 (1906-1990), courtesy name Yangzhai, from Jiangshan, Zhejiang — Dai Li's home county, as Shen notes below with the detail of the dialect used on the telephone. Head of the Xifeng prison 1941-1946. Captured fleeing to Yunnan in December 1949, he was among the war criminals held at Gongdelin with Shen himself; amnestied in 1975, he emigrated to the United States. Corroborated.

于右任 (1879-1964), the veteran revolutionary, head of the Control Yuan and the most celebrated calligrapher of the republic; like Yang a Shaanxi man, which is why a letter to him seemed worth writing. Whether any letter was ever sent, Shen has just told us: Yang tore them all up.

ch07.anchor: The Abode of Rest of the Yangs
ch07.note: 杨氏佳城. 佳城, 'the fine city,' is a classical euphemism for a tomb. The inscription thus carried two of the three characters of Yang Hucheng's name — 杨 and 城, 'city' — and the ornamental column beside it supplied the third: 龙蟠虎踞, 'dragon coiled, tiger crouching' (the stock phrase for a site of imperial strength, coined of Nanking), contains 虎, the tiger of his name. 'My name is all here already.' The English cannot make the characters visible; this note is the best it can do.

李宗仁 (1891-1969), the Guangxi general elected vice-president in 1948, who became acting president when Chiang Kai-shek 'retired' in January 1949. The next chapter of this book is devoted to the plot against him; here it is enough that his order was law to no one, which is Shen's point.

杨森 (1884-1977), the old Sichuan warlord, mayor of Chungking 1948-1949; he followed Chiang to Taiwan and lived to ninety-three. The newspaper episode — the mayor of Chungking professing in print not to know where the Bureau chief was — is of a piece with the documented paralysis of Li Zongren's presidency.

Dai Li, Mao Renfeng and a whole stratum of the service's inner circle came from Jiangshan in Zhejiang, and its nearly impenetrable local speech served them as a ready-made secure channel — a practice documented well beyond this book. That a murder was arranged over the public long-distance line in Jiangshan dialect is as good an illustration as the literature affords.

宋绮云 (1904-1949), Communist Party member from 1927, editor of the Northwest Culture Daily and Yang's confidential secretary. He was seized in 1941; his wife Xu Linxia (徐林侠, 1904-1949), also a Party member, was arrested shortly after, carrying their infant son. Shen's memory slips only in having the boy born in prison: he was eight months old at his mother's arrest. All three died as this chapter tells. Corroborated.

森森 was the pet name of Song Zhenzhong (宋振中, 1941-1949), remembered by all China as 小萝卜头, 'Little Radish-head,' for the outsized head and wasted body prison rations gave him. Raised entirely in captivity, taught by fellow prisoners, he was killed at eight years old — the youngest of the recognized martyrs of the revolution. The date the record gives for the killings in this chapter is 6 September 1949, squarely inside the 'end of August or beginning of September' Shen offers. Corroborated in every particular that can be checked.

麒麟洞, in the Qianling hills outside Guiyang. Standard accounts add a fact Shen omits and his ch. 6 chronology contradicts: Zhang Xueliang himself was held at Qilin Cave for about a year in 1941-1942, between Xiuwen and his move toward Tongzi. The two most famous prisoners of the regime thus passed through the same borrowed villa.

ch07.anchor: the mountain rain about to break and the wind filling the tower
ch07.note: 山雨欲来风满楼, from Xu Hun's Tang poem 'Ascending the East Tower of Xianyang' — the proverbial image of the stillness before a storm. Shen reaches for a literary tag at exactly the moment his plain style fails him; the effect in the original is of a man looking away as he writes.

杨进兴, the Baigongguan head guard who led the knife-work here and served as an executioner again on 27 November. He hid after 1949 under a false name; identified and arrested in 1955, he was tried and shot in Nanking in 1958 — one of the few of this chapter's killers the record follows to an end.

何应钦 (1890-1987), the senior general of the Whampoa establishment, minister of military administration through the war, briefly premier in 1949. His lunch here, pages from a standing order to murder a family, needs no comment; that is presumably why Shen placed the two scenes side by side.

ch07.anchor: the Japanese bandits had taken Dushan
ch07.note: 日寇 — 'Japanese bandits,' the standard wartime and post-war designation, kept as written. Dushan, in southern Guizhou, fell on 2 December 1944 at the farthest tip of the Ichigo offensive; the panic that Guiyang and even Chungking would follow was real and general, and the episode Shen hangs on it — standing orders to kill both generals in the confusion of a retreat — is corroborated in outline by other Juntong memoirs of the contingency plans of that winter.

ch08.note: 叶翔之 (1911-1998), a senior action officer who ran the Bureau's assassination department and, after 1949, rose to head the intelligence services on Taiwan. Shen's aside — that Chiang rejected him for this job as a pen-man who could not kill with his own hands, and demanded Shen instead — is characteristic of how this memoir presents its author: the professional killer's competence is a point of pride even in a confession.

潘其武, Mao Renfeng's office chief and one of the Bureau's senior administrators. That the conference on the plot was held with just four men, the deputy director Xu Zhidao deliberately shut out, is Shen's way of marking how far inside the innermost circle the operation sat.

ch08.anchor: an old hand who had done action work in the Juntong for many years
ch08.note: 'Action work' (行动工作) is the service's euphemism for assassination and abduction, kept as written throughout this book. Shen is describing his own trade. This chapter, written for the CPPCC's historical-materials series, is the fullest first-person confession of a directed political murder in the volume — and its one that failed, which is presumably why he could tell it so completely: no one died, and Li Zongren lived to read it and thank him.

ch08.anchor: search for Dai Li's crashed plane
ch08.note: Dai Li, the Juntong's founding chief, died on 17 March 1946 when his aircraft flew into a hillside near Nanking in bad weather. Shen led the party that reached the wreck. The crash and Shen's role are corroborated; the point here is Chiang invoking that loyalty to bind Shen to the new killing.

ch08.anchor: muster troops and carry out an "armed forcing of the palace"
ch08.note: 逼宫, 'forcing the palace' — the classical term for coercing a ruler to abdicate, here the fear that the Guangxi generals would use their armies to push Chiang out. It is the same charge, 'coercing the supreme commander,' that had been laid on Zhang Xueliang after Xi'an (see the chapter on his detention); Chiang's readiness to kill on the mere suspicion of it is the thread joining these chapters.

张群 (1889-1990), one of Chiang's closest civilian lieutenants, a former premier with long ties to Japan — hence the errand imagined for him here, recruiting Japanese mercenaries. That such a scheme was even weighed in January 1949 is a measure of how far gone the Nationalist position was.

秦景川. Provisional romanization: no independent account of this gunman has been found, and the name is given only as Shen spells it. The bandit assistant is named merely as 'Wang ××' in the source — the surname with the personal name suppressed, exactly as printed — which the translation preserves.
吴德厚, the surveillance man, a graduate of the Juntong's Linli special training class in Hunan (see the note on that class in the Yang Hucheng chapter). Provisional; no outside corroboration found.

ch08.anchor: the natural barrier of the Yangtze
ch08.note: 长江天险, 'the natural moat of the Yangtze,' the classical hope of every southern regime that the great river could be held against an army from the north. The People's Liberation Army crossed it in force in April 1949, within weeks of the deliberations Shen describes, and Nanking fell days later.

美龄号, Chiang Kai-shek's personal aircraft, named for his wife Song Meiling; the 'Zhongmei' (中美号, 'China-America') was another of the presidential planes. The alleged plot — pressing the fitted-out 'Meiling' on the Lis so that it could be shot down as an accident — is Guo Dejie's account as Shen relays it, and is uncorroborated outside these memoirs; Shen's own testimony establishes only that a plan to down Li's plane existed, not that the 'Meiling' was the bait. Read the dinner-table scene as the story the Lis told themselves after reading Shen, not as independently documented fact.

郭德洁 (1906-1966), Li Zongren's wife, who returned with him from the United States to the People's Republic in 1965 — the homecoming that occasions this chapter's coda. She died of cancer in Peking the following year, at the onset of the Cultural Revolution.

Li Zongren, who had gone to the United States in 1949 rather than follow Chiang to Taiwan, returned to the People's Republic in July 1965 in one of the period's great propaganda coups, brokered through intermediaries and personally welcomed by Zhou Enlai. That return is what lets Shen close a confession of a Nationalist murder plot with the intended victim's own voice — and lets him end, in the register the moment required, by adopting the epithet 'Chiang the bandit' from Li's own mouth.

尹冰彦, a functionary of the Revolutionary Committee of the Kuomintang (民革), the organization of former Nationalists who broke with Chiang and remained on the mainland as one of the sanctioned 'democratic parties.' Provisional romanization.

The Selected Historical Materials (文史资料选辑), the CPPCC series for which most of this book was written; see the outline chapter. Shen's citing the exact collection is the memoir marking its own paper trail — and a reminder that these chapters were composed as discrete contributions to that series before being gathered into a book.

蒋贼 and 蒋匪, 'Chiang the bandit / brigand,' the standard mainland epithets of the period, crop-verified against the scan. Shen gives them to Li Zongren, and has Li move over the course of one anecdote from 'Mr. Chiang' to 'Chiang the bandit' — the exact rhetorical arc the 1965 moment demanded of a returning Nationalist, staged here through reported speech. Whether Li spoke the words or Shen supplies them, the register is the evidence.

ch09.anchor: The fourth volume of the *Selected Works of Mao Zedong*
ch09.note: The reference is to Mao's writings of the civil-war years, where the Traffic Police Corps figures among the enemy formations. Opening a chapter by locating its subject in the Selected Works is the clearest possible marker of when and for whom these pages were written: the reader is assumed to have met the corps in Mao first and to need the insider's gloss second.
袖珍王牌军, 'pocket ace army' — Shen's own coinage, kept literal. The image is of a prized elite force in miniature.

雄村, a village on the Xin'an River in Shexian (Huizhou), Anhui — the site of SACO's first training class is well documented, and the village today preserves the class's buildings as a heritage site. Corroborated.

忠义救国军, the guerrilla-cum-secret-service force Dai Li raised around Shanghai in 1937, drawing heavily on the Green Gang; it appears repeatedly in this book (see the outline chapter). The name is conventionally rendered 'Loyal and Patriotic Army' in the SACO literature.

文强 (1907-2001), one of the more famous names to pass through this page: an early Communist who crossed to the Juntong and rose to lieutenant general, captured at Huaihai in 1949. He shared the war-criminals' prison with Shen and, like him, wrote copiously for the historical-materials series after his 1975 amnesty.

汤恩伯 (1898-1954), the Nationalist field commander who held the Linquan class concurrently — the only one of the ten-odd classes not under Dai Li's own name, a mark of how far the SACO training network reached beyond the Juntong proper.

The UD M42, the United Defense 9mm submachine gun that OSS and SACO shipped into China in quantity. The scan prints the roman letters 'UD' bare in the Chinese text; 曲尺 in the same list — literally 'carpenter's square' — is service slang for the ordinary automatic pistol, from its right-angled silhouette, and is rendered accordingly.

吉章简 (1901-1992), first director-general of the postwar Traffic Police administration; Zhou Weilong and Ma Zhichao, who followed him, were both senior Juntong men. The corps' order of battle and its Juntong officering as Shen gives them agree with the published institutional histories; his round figures (twenty corps, forty thousand trained) are of the right order.

ch10.note: 陕甘宁边区, the Communist base area spanning parts of Shaanxi, Gansu and Ningxia, with its capital at Yan'an — the seat of the CCP leadership from 1937 to 1947 and the target of everything in this chapter. Shen writes 'Yenan' throughout in the period English form; the Border Region was its administrative body.

马志超, Shaanxi provincial station chief and Xi'an police chief in the mid-1930s; he reappears later in this book as a director-general of the Traffic Police. The Xi'an special-police training class he ran, and the failed early attempts to seed agents into Yan'an, are consistent with the documented record of Juntong operations against the base area before the war.

张国焘 (1897-1979), one of the founders of the Chinese Communist Party and its representative at its First Congress in 1921, later Mao's chief rival, who lost the power struggle after the Long March and defected to the Nationalists in April 1938. Chiang Kai-shek insisted he be taken into the Juntong, where he was made major-general head of exactly the 'Research Office for Special Political Problems' Shen describes. Outside accounts confirm Shen's portrait in full, down to the disdain: Dai Li treated Zhang as a display piece — proof of Chiang's favour — rather than a useful agent, and Zhang's schemes for turning the Party against itself came to nothing. He left the Juntong after Dai Li's death, and died in a Toronto old-people's home in 1979. Corroborated.
打进拉出, Juntong jargon for the two halves of penetration work: driving agents into the enemy organization, and pulling its members out as defectors. The phrase recurs across this book; kept literal.

洗布坊, 'the cloth-washing works,' a place name at Tongjiaqiao near Ciqikou in Chungking, in the same SACO-adjacent stretch of Gele Mountain country where so much of this book's Chungking apparatus sat. Provisional reading of a degraded scan.

至善里十三号, the address of the Juntong's special detention house in Xi'an. Crop-verified. Zhishanli, 'the lane of reaching goodness,' is one of the mordant accidents of naming this book keeps turning up, like the 'Loyal and Patriotic Army' and the Yangming caves.

沈之岳 (1913-1994), the most successful penetration agent the Juntong ever ran and, on the record, the vindication of everything Dai Li attempted in this chapter and failed at with everyone else. Sent by Dai Li in 1938, he entered Yan'an posing as a progressive student, studied and joined the Party at the Anti-Japanese University, worked in the central organs — Kang Sheng is said to have praised him by name — then served in the New Fourth Army, and returned to Chungking in 1941 with his cover intact. He rose to head Taiwan's intelligence services in the 1960s. His true record is still debated, but the outline Shen gives — the Yan'an trips, the Research Office, the Southeast station posting — matches the standard accounts. Shen Zui's studied vagueness about a man who claimed kinship with him and whose achievement he plainly envied is one of the chapter's quieter tells. Corroborated.

ch10.anchor: claimed kinship with me as a fellow member of the "same clan,"
ch10.note: 同宗, sharing the surname Shen (沈) and so claiming common descent — a customary way of manufacturing intimacy in Republican China. The author Shen Zui and the agent Shen Zhiyue were no relation; the claimed clan-tie is exactly the kind of manufactured trust the chapter is otherwise about.

黄逸公, chief of the Juntong's Northern Shaanxi station at Yulin, on the northern edge of the Border Region. Crop-verified (OCR gave 黄饮公 / 黄锡公). Provisional romanization; no independent account found beyond the scolding Shen records.

程慕颐, chief of the Northwest Special Reconnaissance Station at Hanzhong, and by Shen's account the officer behind the 'poisoning education' and re-infiltration of young people intercepted on the road to Yan'an. Crop-verified; provisional romanization. The detail that he took a detained Communist suspect as a concubine is Shen's, uncorroborated.

抗日军政大学 (抗大 for short), the Chinese People's Anti-Japanese Military and Political University at Yan'an, the cadre school through which tens of thousands of recruits passed — the open door that made Yan'an, in Gong Xianfang's phrase below, 'a chance not to be met with in a thousand years' for an agency trying to slip people in. Shen Zhiyue passed through it; so, this passage says, did the man 'Zhong ××.'

徐佛观 — better known by the name he later took, 徐复观 (1904-1982), who became one of the four great figures of twentieth-century New Confucianism. In these years he was a serving officer and, as here, a Juntong-connected liaison man at the Communist headquarters; the booklet on Yan'an conditions Shen mentions belongs to that phase. His passage from military intelligence to Confucian philosophy is one of the stranger arcs any name in this book carries. Corroborated as to his wartime role.

ch10.anchor: the liaison staff officers posted at the Eighth Route Army headquarters
ch10.note: During the united front the Nationalist command posted liaison officers to the Eighth Route Army; Shen's point is that some of these accredited liaison men were Juntong agents doing intelligence work under diplomatic cover, and that Dai Li debriefed them on how penetration might be improved. Consistent with the documented abuse of the liaison channel by both sides.

梁干乔 (1908-1946), an early Whampoa graduate and one of the founders of the Lixingshe (see the outline chapter), by the early 1940s a commissioner under Hu Zongnan at Yaoxian on anti-Communist work. His account to Shen — dozens of agents a year slipped in through his district disguised as the merchants who traded into the Border Region — is a rare concrete glimpse of the traffic. Provisional beyond the Lixingshe connection.

ch10.anchor: Cheng Yiming, Wu Jingzhong and Huo Liren
ch10.note: 程一鸣, 吴景中 and 霍立人, successive chiefs of the Juntong's Northwest region at Lanzhou. Cheng Yiming was in fact a long-buried Communist agent inside the Juntong, a fact unknown to Shen and unmentionable when he wrote; 吴景中 is the historical original of Wu Jingzhong / 'Wu Zhi'guo' in later spy fiction. Shen presents all three flatly as colleagues, which is what they were to him. Romanizations provisional except where attested elsewhere.

于斌 (1901-1978), the prominent and militantly anti-Communist Catholic bishop of Nanking, later the first Chinese cardinal (1969) and rector of Fu Jen University in Taiwan. His wartime closeness to the Nationalist security apparatus is well documented; Shen's account of his offer to build a Juntong network in the Border Region through Catholic congregations is uncorroborated in the specifics but entirely in character. Crop-verified (OCR gave 于研).

蒋更生, one of the assassination team Dai Li sent toward Yan'an in 1942 and a student Shen had trained. The whole assassination programme this section describes — repeated teams dispatched, all arrested or vanished, not one result — is Shen's inside testimony and is not independently documented; it should be read as a participant's account of a failed secret operation, credible in outline (the CCP's counter-intelligence at Yan'an was formidable) but unverifiable in its particulars.

龚仙舫, the Juntong personnel chief, crop-verified against a scan that mangled the name five different ways (黎/获/缆/约/奢仙盘). It is Gong who, across this chapter, supplies Shen — and the reader — with the clearest statement of the long-infiltration doctrine: plant people for years, let them inch in, wait for Yan'an's open recruitment. Provisional romanization.

徐业道, the Juntong action chief who, Shen notes pointedly, had come up through judicial work and was 'a layman at action' — hence the argument over whether one man could carry out a shooting. The scene is Shen the professional killer correcting his own superiors on tradecraft, and being overruled: one of the chapter's clearest instances of the competence-as-pride register flagged in the Li Zongren chapter.

龙飞虎 (1915-1999), a real bodyguard of Zhou Enlai's through the war years, later a PLA general. That Shen should remember this one name from a Juntong survey of Communist leaders' bodyguards — 'because the man's name was rather unusual' (龙飞虎, 'dragon flying tiger') — is corroborated at least to the extent that Long Feihu was indeed Zhou's guard. The survey of leaders' security details as a preliminary to assassination is Shen's testimony alone.

袁寄滨, a secretary of the Juntong secretariat, Shen's fellow Xiangtan townsman, in whose room Shen says he happened on the bodyguard survey. Crop-verified (OCR gave 袁寡滨). Provisional romanization; the anecdote rests entirely on Shen's word.

ch11.anchor: a pair of dogs loyal to Chiang Kai-shek
ch11.note: 忠于蒋介石的走狗, 'running dogs loyal to Chiang Kai-shek.' 走狗 ('running dog,' lackey) is the standard period term of abuse, kept literal. Shen applies it here to Dai Li and Hu Zongnan — and, by the logic of the memoir, to the class of men he was one of.

宏恩医院, the Country Hospital, a foreign-run hospital in the Shanghai International Settlement — which explains Shen's remark that few Chinese went there and Dai Li was the only Chinese on his floor. Dai Li's 1937 appendicitis and Song Meiling's visit are the kind of detail only an insider supplies; uncorroborated in the specifics but unremarkable.
陈质平, then a Shanghai special-district inspector, later a Nationalist diplomat. Provisional romanization.

西北王, 'King of the Northwest,' Hu Zongnan's universal nickname, reflecting the near-viceregal military and civil power he held over Shaanxi and the approaches to the Communist base. Kept as the epithet it was.

熊斌 (1894-1964), a senior Nationalist general who was chairman of Shaanxi province in the mid-1940s. Crop-verified (OCR gave 熊汪). The plot to replace him with the 'noted executioner' Zhu Shaozhou, and its exposure through the agent Zuo Ming, is Shen's account; the personalities are real, the episode uncorroborated in outside sources.

祝绍周 (1892-1968), a Zhejiang general who did in fact serve as chairman of Shaanxi later in the 1940s — so the recommendation Shen describes was, in the event, realized. Provisional beyond the fact of his governorship.

左明, the Juntong agent whose leak Shen recounts — a fellow of Dai Li's own detachment in the sixth Whampoa class. He appears again in the Chungking chapter (ch03) in the same episode of the leaked appointment. Provisional romanization.

俞作柏 (1889-1959), a Guangxi general who had briefly been chairman of Guangxi province in 1929 before being driven out — which is the 'real capacity' Dai Li had heard of. His command of the Loyal and Patriotic Army and Dai's disappointment in him are Shen's inside account. Corroborated as to the man; the command episode is uncorroborated.

德造二十响驳壳枪, the C96 'broomhandle' Mauser in its detachable-magazine, twenty-round form — the 'box cannon' (驳壳枪) that was the status sidearm of Republican officers and gunmen alike. That Dai Li kept a private collection of pistols and gave his best away to flatter Hu is the sort of texture only a subordinate who handled the armoury would record.

ch11.anchor: sixty or seventy female students he had recruited in Changsha
ch11.note: The Central Military Academy's Seventh Branch (中央军校七分校) was Hu Zongnan's own training establishment near Xi'an; that he funneled recruits — including young women — into Dai Li's Linli agent-training class is consistent with the documented traffic between Hu's and Dai's organizations, though the specific gift Shen describes is his own testimony.

ch11.anchor: He Yingqin, Qian Dajun, Lin Wei and Yu Jishi
ch11.note: Four pillars of the Nationalist high command whose birthdays and festivals Dai Li worked as occasions for gift-diplomacy on Hu's behalf: He Yingqin, the war minister (see the Yang Hucheng chapter); Qian Dajun (钱大钧, 1893-1982), Chiang's chief aide and a head of the Attendants' Office; Lin Wei (林蔚, 1889-1955), a senior staff general; and Yu Jishi (俞济时, 1904-1990), long the commander of Chiang's bodyguard. The list is a map of whom it paid to cultivate.

叶霞翟 (1913-1981), whom the book writes 叶霞弟 and whose given name, Shen says, Dai Li elegantized from 弟 to 履 (the standard form is 翟). The corroborated outline matches Shen: she was Dai Li's student at the Hangzhou police school, studied at Guanghua University in Shanghai, took a doctorate at Wisconsin, and married Hu Zongnan in 1947 after a long engagement. Two of Shen's colourings are disputed by later accounts — that she did intelligence work (her family says she never did) and the insinuation, pressed harder elsewhere in his writings, that she had been Dai Li's mistress. Read the passage as an interested man's version of a marriage he helped broker.

光华大学, a patriotic private university founded in Shanghai in 1925 by students and staff who walked out of the missionary St. John's after the May Thirtieth incident; it was absorbed into East China Normal University after 1949. Ye Xiadi both studied there and, Shen says, was installed as a professor there for the political usefulness of the title.

刘健群 (1902-1972), a Nationalist politician close to the Blue Shirts / Lixingshe current and later president of the Legislative Yuan; the Nanking-house dispute Shen recounts, with Liu's wife camping at the gate, is a piece of insider comedy uncorroborated outside the memoir. Provisional beyond the man's identity.

舍我其谁, 'if not me, then who' — a phrase from Mencius, the classic expression of a man's sense of unique destiny, here in Hu Zongnan's mouth about ruling the army. Shen deploys the Mencian tag to make Hu's arrogance ring; kept with its force.

ch11.anchor: Wei Daming, Yue Zhuyuan, Ruan Qingyuan, Xie Ligong, Wang Yixin
ch11.note: Senior Juntong men sent for general-officer training so as to acquire regular-army rank. Wei Daming (魏大铭, 1907-1998) is the notable one: the Juntong's radio and cryptography chief, the technical brain behind its signals intelligence, later head of Nationalist communications intelligence on Taiwan. Crop-verified (OCR gave 魏大铬). The rest are provisional.

陈洁如 (1906-1971), whom Chiang Kai-shek married in 1921 and set aside in 1927 to marry Song Meiling; she was sent to America and lived quietly thereafter. Shen writes 蒋介石的另一个老婆, 'Chiang Kai-shek's other wife' — the phrase is kept as he wrote it, neither upgraded to 'former wife' nor softened, since the flat designation is itself evidence of how the arrangement was regarded. That Chiang's discarded wife, younger son and elder brother were parcelled out to Hu and Dai to 'look after' is Shen's account of how the two men made themselves indispensable; uncorroborated in the particulars.

蒋纬国 (1916-1997), Chiang Kai-shek's adopted younger son (his natural father was Dai Jitao), a career armoured-forces officer. His being placed in Hu Zongnan's care fits the documented fact that he served under Hu in the Northwest during the war.

The Nanking address where Dai Li's body lay after the crash of 17 March 1946 (see the Yang Hucheng chapter for the crash). Hu Zongnan's grief-stricken rush to the coffin is Shen's eyewitness account; the closeness of the two men is corroborated by every history of the period.

ch11.anchor: among Hu Zongnan's secretary and the head of his Northwest news agency were Communist Party members
ch11.note: This is the chapter's most historically charged passage. The most famous Communist in Hu Zongnan's secretariat was Xiong Xianghui (熊向晖), Zhou Enlai's deep-cover agent, who served as Hu's confidential secretary and in 1943 passed out Hu's plan to attack the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region — the very campaign the previous chapter describes. Xiong was one of a network (with Shen Jian and Chen Zhongjing, the 'latter three heroes'); all left Hu's staff for study abroad around May 1947, months before the autumn-1947 discovery Shen dates here. Crucially, none was caught: Xiong's cover held until he revealed himself in 1949. So Shen's account — that the Juntong 'found' Communists at Hu's side and that Hu suppressed it to save face — is best read as the security service belatedly detecting the network's traces after its members had already gone, which is consistent with the documented history and makes Hu's panic, and his cover-up, entirely comprehensible. Corroborated in its essentials; Shen did not know, or does not say, that the greatest of these agents had slipped the net.

范长江 (1909-1970), the celebrated journalist whose reportage from the Northwest and the Red areas made his name in the 1930s; he secretly joined the CCP in 1939 and became a leading figure in Communist journalism after 1949. Hu Zongnan's admission that he had recommended Fan to Chiang without knowing he was a Communist — and been scolded for it — is a nicely humiliating detail; the general fact of Fan's Communist allegiance is well documented.

ch11.anchor: Chen Cheng had always been on bad terms
ch11.note: 胡宗南 and 陈诚 (Chen Cheng, Chiang's other great military favourite and by 1949 the master of Taiwan) were long-standing rivals within the Nationalist command — which is why, Shen explains, Hu would rather have sent his family to Kunming than to Chen Cheng's Taiwan. The rivalry is well attested; in the event Hu sent them to Taiwan anyway, as the mainland collapsed.

卢汉 (1895-1974), the Yunnan provincial chairman, who stalled Mao Renfeng's demand to massacre progressives in Kunming and in December 1949 declared for the Communists, taking Yunnan over to the People's Republic by peaceful uprising. Shen's frustration here is the losing side's; Lu Han's obstruction was the prelude to the defection. Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: more than the bamboo can hold
ch12.note: 罄竹难书, 'so many the bamboo (writing slips) could not record them all' — a classical idiom for crimes past counting, from the charge-sheet against the tyrant of Sui. Kept close to the literal image.

ch12.anchor: he actually picked the pocket of his own ancestor
ch12.note: 扒到他老祖宗的头上, 'picked the pocket of his own ancestor / grand-master' — the joke turns on Shen having been, as detective-squad captain, the presiding authority over the whole thieving world: the pickpocket's professional 'ancestor.' A rare flash of the memoir's humour, and Shen enjoying his old eminence.

黑话, 'black speech,' the cant of the underworld — the specialized in-group vocabulary this whole chapter is partly a glossary of. The trade-terms that follow (eating hard money, running the wheels, peeling the dew) are the argot itself; they are translated for sense with the literal image kept, since the images are the point.

ch12.anchor: "the thief has his thieving mates, the robber his robbing crew."
ch12.note: 贼有贼伴，盗有盗伙 — a rhyming proverb of the trade, kept in parallel form to preserve its jingle.

ch12.anchor: the Subei gang (also called the Jiangbei gang)
ch12.note: 苏北帮/江北帮, the gang of migrants from the poorer country north of the Yangtze (Subei / Jiangbei), long the lowest-status group in Shanghai's labour hierarchy and stereotyped as its criminal underclass. The gang geography Shen lays out — local, Subei, Anhui, Zhejiang, Cantonese — maps Shanghai's actual immigrant strata.

吃硬钱, cant for making one's living by force (robbery), as against 吃洋火钱 ('eating match-money,' picking pockets — the nimble-fingered trade) and the snatch-and-run lines below. 吃 X 钱, 'to eat X money,' is the underworld's general formula for 'to earn by the X method.' The renderings keep the eating-metaphor because the whole taxonomy runs on it.

扳枝, literally 'to pull the branch' — cant for informing on or turning out a freelancer who works outside the gang system. Provisional reading of a degraded, argot term; the sense (the trade polices its own) is clear from context.

ch12.anchor: "Green the first time, familiar the second, expert the third"
ch12.note: 一回生，二回熟，三回精 — an ordinary Chinese proverb about learning by repetition, here turned to a grim use: the prison as the thieves' training academy, each sentence an apprenticeship. Kept in its three-beat form.

亮相, a term from opera — the pose an actor strikes on first coming onstage — used here for the old hand's ritual of establishing his standing on entering a cell. The nail-in-the-wall performance that follows is the 'entrance.' The same word 亮相 recurs as the thing a top pickpocket most avoids: being made to show his face.

吃讲茶, 'eating tea to talk it over' — the Jianghu institution of settling disputes by formal negotiation over tea, presided over by gang elders, in place of (or before) violence. A real and documented custom of the Shanghai underworld, not a metaphor.
强者为王, 'the strong is king' — the frank law of the Jianghu, which Shen extends, pointedly, to the society at large that produced it.

十六铺, the great wharf district on the Huangpu at the edge of Shanghai's old city — the landing-point for river traffic and one of the classic turfs of the dock-and-boat underworld. It recurs below as where the murdered-boat case ends.

阿狗, 'Ah Dog' — a deliberately lowly, unlucky-sounding milk-name (dogs, being cheap, were thought hard for demons to covet), of the kind given to children so they would be easy to raise. That a fifty-year-old crime boss still went by it is itself a piece of underworld texture.

ch12.anchor: a girl still at middle school, only a little over ten years old
ch12.note: One of the chapter's few undercutting human moments: the master pickpocket Tang Zong wants paraded turns out to be a schoolgirl, and Shen, uncharacteristically, covers for her. Whether the anecdote is exact or improved in the telling, its function in the 1962-66 frame is to show the old society making criminals of children — but the tenderness reads as Shen's own.

下江帮, 'down-river gangs' — 下江 ('lower river,' the Yangtze delta: Shanghai, Nanking, Jiangsu) was the wartime Sichuanese name for the refugees who flooded up-river to Chungking. The 'down-river gangs' were thus the delta underworld transplanted to the wartime capital, working outside the local networks the police had penetrated.

王胡子, 'Wang the Bearded,' original name Wang He (crop-verified; OCR gave 王稚). A master-thief figure of a familiar Jianghu type — the retired great robber living in respectable ease under police protection, still commanding his old apprentices and still, quietly, the guarantor of the property he no longer steals. Whether a single historical man or a composite, the portrait is drawn from life; uncorroborable by name.

ch12.anchor: the abbot's room in Longhua Temple was burgled
ch12.note: 龙华寺, the ancient Buddhist temple in southern Shanghai, by its famous pagoda — and, grimly, next to the Songhu Garrison Headquarters, whose commander Yang Hu (see ch02) was himself a gang overlord. The theft of a jade Buddha and gold ritual vessels from so guarded a place, solved only by appeal to the retired master-thief, is the chapter's set-piece; uncorroborated but characteristic.
洗手, 'washed his hands' — the standard Jianghu term for retiring from the trade (the fuller form 金盆洗手, 'washing one's hands in a golden basin'). The English idiom happens to match, and is kept.

ch12.anchor: "fly along the eaves and walk the walls"
ch12.note: 飞檐走壁, the stock wuxia phrase for the rooftop agility of the knight-errant — which Shen, having had a captured burglar demonstrate, debunks: it was all done with tools. The passage is the memoir puncturing its own culture's romance of the flying thief, and the tool descriptions that follow (the 'soft pole,' the 'hard pole,' the rubber-and-diamond glass trick) are a real burglar's kit.
丈, ten Chinese feet, about 3.3 metres; the extending 'hard pole' reached three metres and more.

ch12.anchor: "A distant thief must have a near nest."
ch12.note: 远贼必有近窝, a proverb of the trade: however far a thief travels, he must lodge and fence his goods locally — which is exactly the seam the detectives worked. Kept in its proverb form.

梁华盛 (1904-1978), a real Nationalist general (later a full general on Taiwan); the honey-trap robbery Shen recounts, whatever its exact truth, is told at the expense of a named senior officer, which is part of the chapter's levelling relish. Provisional beyond the man's identity.

守株待兔, 'guarding the tree-stump waiting for a hare' — from a Han-dynasty parable of the farmer who, having once seen a hare run into a stump and die, gave up farming to wait for another; proverbial for passive, luck-dependent method. Shen applies it, self-deprecatingly, to his own celebrated detective work — waiting at the Wealth God temple for the culprit to appear.

财神庙: the god of wealth (财神) was worshipped across all trades, but a shrine kept up specifically by prostitutes and 'swindle-women' to bless their takings is a sardonic detail of the demimonde. The 'swindle-women' (拆白党, below) redeeming vows there after a successful con is the sort of thing only an insider informer-network would know.

拆白党, the Shanghai term for confidence-tricksters who fleeced men through seduction — here the female practitioners, of whom the honey-trap robber of General Liang was one. A well-documented category of Republican Shanghai's underworld.
司蒂倍克, the transliteration of Studebaker, the American car — a marker of the con's expensive staging, and of the period's brand vocabulary. Kept as the make it names.
瞎猫捉耗子, the fuller proverb being 瞎猫碰上死耗子, 'a blind cat stumbling on a dead mouse' — pure luck, not skill. Shen uses it, again, to deflate his own reputation for lightning detective work.

盐城, a city in the Subei (northern Jiangsu) region; the doorkeeper's origin there, plus Mauser cartridge cases, is the forensic reasoning by which Shen pins the post-office robbery on the Subei gang — a nice illustration of the gang-geography set out at the chapter's start.

驳壳枪, 'box-shell gun' — the C96 Mauser, whose wooden holster doubled as a shoulder stock; the workhorse pistol of Chinese soldiers and bandits alike. Shen's point is a real one of criminal forensics: city thieves favoured small concealable pistols, out-of-town robbers the longer-ranged, harder-hitting Mauser, so the weapon fingerprinted the gang.

葆哥, an affectionate-respectful gang address (given-name + 哥, 'elder brother') for the inspectorate section-head Hu Baowen, who ran protection for the very bandits he was paid to catch. The nickname marks how thoroughly the detective had become one of the fraternity.

替罪羊, 'substitute-crime goat' — the exact calque of the Biblical scapegoat, long naturalized in Chinese. Here two hired peasant porters are executed in place of the real robbers as part of the deal between detective and gang: the chapter's coldest single image of how 'cases were cracked.'

ch12.anchor: the Henry-Edward or the Battley system
ch12.note: Two real fingerprint-classification systems: the Henry system (developed under Edward Henry, the basis of British and colonial practice) and the Battley system (Harry Battley's single-fingerprint method, Scotland Yard, 1930s). Shen's point is that the Nationalist forces never standardized on either — each school of foreign-trained officers pushed its own — so the 'scientific' apparatus was a shambles. Corroborated as to the systems' existence.

测谎器, the polygraph, among the American criminal-investigation equipment supplied to the Nationalists after 1945. Shen's verdict — useless against habitual thieves, where a few words of argot from a veteran worked instantly — is the memoir's recurring contrast between imported technique and native tradecraft, and here it doubles as a jab at the American patrons.

ch12.anchor: "he who steals a hook is put to death, he who steals a state is made a lord."
ch12.note: 窃钩者诛，窃国者侯 — from the Zhuangzi: the petty thief is executed while the man who usurps a kingdom becomes a feudal lord. The classic Chinese epigram on the class character of law, and Shen turns it, in the self-criticism register, against the reactionary state he served. Its placement is deliberate.

ch12.anchor: the seventh brigade captain of the Shanghai Garrison Headquarters inspectorate, Xiao Fuquan
ch12.note: 肖复权 (also written 萧复权), a real Juntong-linked Shanghai security officer of the late 1940s. The Sun Ke burglary anecdote — the court, unable to torture, referring the recanting thief back to the police to be beaten into re-confessing — is Shen's, and stands as his indictment of the whole 'lawful' apparatus. Provisional beyond the man's identity.

ch12.anchor: Sun Ke's mansion at No. 22 Columbia Road
ch12.note: 孙科 (Sun Ke / Sun Fo, 1891-1973), the son of Sun Yat-sen and president of the Legislative Yuan — 'the great president' of the passage. Columbia Road (哥伦比亚路, now Panyu Road) was in Shanghai's western villa district. That a burglary at Sun Ke's house bent the whole judicial machinery to please him is Shen's illustration of law serving rank.

胜利大厦, a Chungking landmark of the war years; the pickpocketing of the SACO chief of staff Bei Leli there, wallet-and-chain and all, and Dai Li's fury at the loss of face before his American master, is the chapter's comic mirror of the Tang Zong episode at its start. The ivory seal 'carved with a Chinese name' that Dai had given Bei Leli is a period detail of Sino-American secret-service fraternizing.

老虎凳, the 'tiger bench' — a torture in which the victim's legs are bound flat to a bench and bricks forced under the heels until the knees break backward; one of the signature tortures of the Nationalist secret police, notorious from the Red Crag literature. Shen lists it flatly among the methods 'experimented' on a dock porter, which is the register the chapter works in: atrocity recorded as procedure.

活教材, 'living teaching material' — Shen's term, kept as written, for the petty thieves on whom Juntong trainees practised torture so as to be ready to use it on Communists and democrats. It is among the book's most damning single phrases, and its flat, pedagogical tone is exactly the evidence the apparatus of this edition exists to preserve: he is confessing, and the confession's coldness is the point.

老闸捕房, the Louza (Laozha) police station of the Shanghai International Settlement, on Nanjing Road — the same station outside which the May Thirtieth shootings of 1925 took place. A Chinese detective there, riding on foreign power to beat a rickshaw-puller to death and then defy the courts, is Shen's case-study in the impunity of the Concession police.

ch12.anchor: a saddle made of human skin
ch12.note: The single most gothic item in the book: a western-Hunan bandit chief's gift to the garrison inspectorate head Huang Jiachi, made from the flayed skin of a man Huang had had killed. Shen offers it, with the disclaimer that he would not have believed it unshown, as the outer limit of what the wartime security-and-bandit symbiosis produced. Uncorroborable, and presented as such.

ch12.anchor: Li Huchen, after killing the owner of a bathhouse
ch12.note: A different Li Huchen (李虎臣) from the general who held Xi'an in the Yang Hucheng chapter — here a Chungking inspectorate detective who murdered a bathhouse owner to seize the business. The identical characters are a coincidence of common name; noted to prevent the two being read as one man.

ch13.anchor: the open merger of the American and Chiang secret services
ch13.note: 美蒋特务公开合流. This chapter is the fullest account in the book of SACO — the Sino-American Special Technical Cooperative Organization (Chinese 中美特种技术合作所; the English name it actually used was 'Sino-American Cooperative Organization'). Founded 1943, dissolved 1946, headed by Dai Li with the US Navy's Milton Miles as deputy, it trained and armed tens of thousands of Nationalist guerrillas and secret police and ran weather, signals and intelligence operations against Japan. Its role in equipping the forces that fought the Communists after 1945, and its prisons at Baigongguan and Zhazidong, made it a byword in the People's Republic for American complicity in the Nationalist terror. Shen's insider account is broadly corroborated by the Western scholarship (Frederic Wakeman's Spymaster; Miles's own memoir A Different Kind of War), which of course frames it very differently.

ch13.anchor: head of the General Affairs Department of the Juntong bureau
ch13.note: Shen states his own position and his reason for knowing SACO from the inside: as head of general affairs he handled its housing, supply and entertaining. The chapter is therefore first-person testimony from within the joint organization — its evidentiary value and its self-interest both at their highest. Note the closing appeal that surviving participants correct and supplement him: the 文史资料 mode of collective participant testimony, written to be revised by others who were there.

ch13.anchor: passed the information to Xiao Bo
ch13.note: 萧勃 (the book prints 肖勃), the Juntong's man in Washington under diplomatic cover. The Pearl Harbor anecdote — that the Juntong's cipher-breakers warned of Japanese Pacific intentions and were laughed off until December 8 — is Shen's, and is the founding myth SACO's creation was hung on; it appears in Miles's memoir too, from the other side. Treat it as the origin story both partners told, not as established fact.

杨宣诚, then head of the Second (intelligence) Bureau of the Ministry of Military Operations; a naval officer and one of the Nationalists' senior intelligence men. His presence, with Zheng Jiemin and the air-force chief Zhou Zhirou, at Dai Li's first dinner for the American attaché marks how the whole intelligence establishment was mobilized to court the Americans.
周至柔 (1899-1986), commander-in-chief of the Nationalist air force, later chief of the general staff and governor of Taiwan. Crop-verified (OCR gave 周至条).

黑室, 'Black Chamber' — the generic Chinese term for a cryptanalysis bureau, from Herbert Yardley's famous American 'Black Chamber' (Yardley in fact worked for Chiang's government in Chungking in 1938-40). Shen's account of each side trying to learn the other's cipher methods while withholding its own is the authentic texture of 'cooperation' between rival services.

Henry Luce (1898-1967), founder of Time and Life, born in China to missionary parents and the most powerful pro-Nationalist voice in American media. That Roosevelt's 'personal representative' at the signing was the press magnate Luce, alongside Navy Secretary Frank Knox, is corroborated and tells its own story about the China lobby. Knox (诺克斯) was US Secretary of the Navy 1940-44.

ch13.anchor: the standing vice-minister of foreign affairs, Hu Shize
ch13.note: 胡世泽 (1894-1972), a career diplomat who later served as a UN under-secretary-general. He signed in place of T. V. Soong, who was Foreign Minister.

ch13.anchor: chief of staff Bei Leli, chief secretary Smith
ch13.note: 贝乐利, rendered 'Bei Leli' throughout this book; the transliteration is provisional and the exact American name is not established from the scan. He was SACO's American chief of staff and acted as deputy director after Miles was removed in 1945.

ch13.anchor: eighth-department head Shen Zui all attend
ch13.note: 沈醉 — the author, naming himself in the third person in the roster of those present, exactly as he does elsewhere in the book. Crop-verified against the scan (OCR gave 沈酬). The eighth department was the one he headed.

The contract terms Shen reconstructs — that the Juntong supplied all the intelligence while the Americans supplied none, that 'other relevant intelligence' was the clause under which anti-Communist and anti-Soviet material flowed, that fifty thousand agents were to be armed — are consistent in substance with what the Western scholarship documents of SACO, though Shen is reconstructing the text from memory a decade and more later and says so.

William J. 'Wild Bill' Donovan (1883-1959), head of the Office of Strategic Services, the wartime forerunner of the CIA. His running struggle with the Navy's Miles for control of American intelligence in China — a central theme of this chapter's later section — is one of the best-documented turf wars of the war, and Shen's inside view of it from the Chinese side is a genuine contribution.

ch13.anchor: Admiral Cooke, commander of the American Seventh Fleet
ch13.note: Admiral Charles M. Cooke (柯克), a senior US Navy commander in the postwar Western Pacific and a strong supporter of the Nationalists in the civil war. Doubling the number of senior Juntong agents sent to train in America was exactly the kind of postwar aid the Communists cited as proof of American intervention.

ch13.anchor: The armed secret-service forces the Juntong led numbered fifty or sixty thousand
ch13.note: SACO's arming of roughly fifty thousand Nationalist guerrillas and secret police — the 'rice-paddy navy' of Miles's memoir — is corroborated; these forces became the Traffic Police Corps of the previous chapter and fought in the civil war. Shen's figure and the reorganization into the Traffic Police are both borne out by the record.

王芃生 (1893-1946), head of the Institute for International Affairs, the Nationalists' Japan-intelligence and research body; a genuine Japan specialist. Crop-verified (OCR gave 王苞生). His supplying propaganda material to SACO's psychological-warfare section is in character.

ch13.anchor: Xie was a Trotskyite renegade who had been Chen Duxiu's secretary
ch13.note: Chen Duxiu (陈独秀, 1879-1942) was a founder and the first general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, expelled in 1929 as a 'Trotskyite.' That the head of SACO's psychological-warfare section was a former secretary of his who had defected to the Juntong is Shen's claim; the man is left unnamed in the scan. Miles's reported delight at employing such a man is the sort of detail Shen deploys to characterize both partners.

林可胜 (1897-1969), the eminent physiologist Robert Kho-Seng Lim, founder of the Chinese Red Cross Medical Relief Corps and surgeon-general of the Nationalist army — a figure of real international standing. Shen's note that Lim's nominee Zhang Yuehan quit SACO the moment he grasped what it was is a rare instance in the chapter of someone recoiling from the organization.

ch13.anchor: many of the martyrs shot down still wore these on their hands and feet
ch13.note: The November 1949 Chungking massacre at the Baigongguan and Zhazidong prisons inside the SACO compound (see the preface and the Yang Hucheng chapter). Shen's detail — that the murdered prisoners wore the very American handcuffs SACO had supplied — is the chapter's bluntest statement of the through-line from the 'cooperation' to the killings, and the reason SACO's name carried the weight it did in the People's Republic.

顾祝同 (1893-1987), commander of the Nationalist Third War Zone — the general responsible for the New Fourth Army Incident of 1941. His speaking at the first Sino-American class's opening places a senior field commander at the birth of the American-trained secret-service forces.

ch13.anchor: the disappearance of the Zhejiang University professor Fei Gong
ch13.note: This is the chapter's, and perhaps the book's, most damning passage — for what Shen does NOT say. Fei Gong (费巩, 1905-1945), the liberal Zhejiang University professor of political science, was abducted at the Qiansimen dock in Chungking on 5 March 1945 and murdered, his body destroyed in nitric acid (the same 镪水 used on Yang Hucheng) — and the interrogation records of captured Nationalist agents established that it was SACO agents who did it. Shen conducted, by his own account here, a nearly two-month 'search' for Fei across Guizhou and the Wushan gorges, and ends by calling the case 'a mystery.' It was no mystery: he was searching, in a piece of theatre staged to satisfy the American general Wedemeyer and forty petitioning professors, for a man his own organization had killed. Whether Shen genuinely did not know in 1945, or knew and could not or would not say when he wrote, the passage stands as the sharpest illustration in the book of the limits of even a confessional memoir — and the apparatus of this edition exists precisely to mark the gap between what the page says and what the record shows. Fei Gong was declared a revolutionary martyr in 1978.

竺可桢 (1890-1974), the great meteorologist and geographer, president of Zhejiang University 1936-1949, who moved the university across wartime China to Zunyi and Meitan (the 'Zhejiang University Long March'). His impatience with Shen and Clark, and his pointed advice to go back and ask the government's own prisons, reads — in light of what SACO had done — as a man who understood exactly what had happened to his professor and said as much to his face.

ch13.anchor: the American Far East theatre chief of staff Wedemeyer
ch13.note: General Albert Wedemeyer (魏德迈, 1897-1989), who replaced Stilwell (史迪威) as US commander in the China theatre in 1944; a strong Nationalist partisan. His pressure to place SACO under Army/OSS control against the Navy's Miles, recounted in the next section, is well documented. That he threw his weight behind rescuing an American-educated professor — while the organization under dispute had murdered the man — is an irony Shen leaves for the reader.

希姆莱: Heinrich Himmler, head of the SS and the Gestapo. That Roosevelt at the Cairo Conference (November 1943) asked to meet Dai Li — 'this Chinese Himmler' — is an anecdote that recurs in the SACO literature; the comparison of Dai Li to Himmler was current among Americans at the time. Whether Roosevelt used the phrase, the point for Shen is Miles's role in building Dai Li's standing with 'the master of his master.'

Miles's personal seven-star pennant is documented — it was the SACO emblem Miles flew.
