Shen's lurid origin story (that the seven stars commemorated seven bullet holes in a boat of Filipino insurgents Miles machine-gunned) is uncorroborated and almost certainly Juntong lore or Shen's own embroidery. Presented here as the tale Shen was told, and a measure of how Miles was mythologized inside the Juntong.

驼峰: the air route over the eastern Himalayas from India to China, the Allies' only supply line into China after the Burma Road was cut. Shen's account — two thousand Navy men stranded in India unable to fly the Hump because the Army would not lift them — is his Chinese-side view of the Army-Navy feud that the American records also describe.

The two atrocities Shen recounts to illustrate Miles's 'sham-democratic' management style — the gang-rape settled with a month's leave-ban and hush money, the attempted assault brushed off with a laugh — are uncorroborable individually but are offered as Shen's eyewitness testimony to how SACO's American personnel behaved toward the local population and how the Juntong police covered for them. The register is worth marking: Shen reports these as illustrations of Miles's cleverness with subordinates, not primarily as crimes against the women.

任福根, an American SACO agent (a former missionary, a 'China hand') whom Shen says was arrested for espionage after 1949 and held until 1956 — one of the American SACO personnel caught up in the People's Republic's postwar spy cases, which Shen cites as proof of SACO's lasting network. Provisional transliteration of the name.

ch14.note: Long Yun (1884-1962), the Yi 'King of Yunnan,' governed the province as a near-autonomous fief from 1927 until Chiang Kai-shek removed him by armed force in the October 1945 Kunming coup and installed Lu Han. His long rule is why Yunnan entered 1949 with a leadership not simply Chiang's creature.

The Democratic League leaders Li Gongpu (shot 11 July 1946, died the next dawn) and Wen Yiduo (machine-gunned 15 July 1946, eight bullets) were assassinated in Kunming by agents of the Bureau's Kunming station. The book's attribution to the secret services is corroborated by mainstream PRC accounts; a principal gunman, Cai Yunqi, was caught in 1957 and executed in 1958. Shen elsewhere in his memoirs tried to complicate the Juntong's responsibility, but the killings are firmly documented as secret-service work.

Li Mi (1902-1973), Nationalist 8th Army commander at Kunming. After the Yunnan collapse he led remnant troops into Burma and became a warlord of the opium-growing Golden Triangle, sustained for years by covert Nationalist and foreign support.

Yu Chengwan (1902-1955) had won fame commanding the 74th Army's 57th Division in the 1943 defence of Changde; by 1949 he led the 26th Army at Kunming. His hostility to the peaceful liberation, and his manoeuvres once detained, run through this chapter's climax.

Long Live the Tiger Braves (Hufen wansui, 1945) by the popular novelist Zhang Henshui, on Yu Chengwan's defence of Changde. 'Tiger Braves' (虎贲) is an ancient term for elite palace guards, here the 57th Division's code name. Often called China's first modern documentary war novel, it was commissioned by Yu himself; corroborated accounts note the division held Changde with some eight thousand men, of whom only about eighty survived.

The September 9 affair (九九整肃): on 9 September 1949, Nationalist secret services under Xu Yuanju carried out mass arrests in Kunming, detaining several hundred, with roughly two hundred marked for death, to cut off Lu Han's line of retreat toward the Communists. Lu Han stalled the executions and, after acting president Li Zongren's assent, had all those held released. The account here is corroborated by later PRC sources, in which Shen figures as one of the planners.

Chiang Ching-kuo (1910-1988), Chiang Kai-shek's son and future president of the Republic of China on Taiwan, here acting as his father's fixer over the Kunming secret services and the plan to hold, and if need be kill, Lu Han.

ch14.anchor: forty-four people led by Huang Shaohong
ch14.note: On 13 August 1949 forty-four figures in Hong Kong, led by Huang Shaohong of the New Guangxi Clique and including Long Yun, issued the declaration Our Understanding of and Position on the Present Stage of the Chinese Revolution, breaking with Chiang and endorsing Communist leadership. Chiang expelled them from the party and issued warrants; the count of forty-four is corroborated.

Yang Jie (1889-1949), a Nationalist general and military theorist who had turned toward the Communists. The killing Shen was ordered to carry out here was done in Hong Kong in September 1949 after Yang fled Kunming; the book treats it directly in a later chapter. Shen's claim that he dragged his feet is his own; the deed itself is documented.

ch14.anchor: beat the grass and startle the snake
ch14.note: Beat the grass and startle the snake (打草惊蛇): to alert an enemy by a careless move, so that a later blow misses its mark.
Turtles in the jar (瓮中之鳖): trapped with no escape; the image is of a soft-shelled turtle in a narrow-mouthed urn.
A mantis stopping a chariot (螳臂挡车): to pit hopelessly inadequate force against an overwhelming one.

Lu Han's uprising (卢汉起义). Late on 9 December 1949, having lured the senior Nationalist commanders — Li Mi, Yu Chengwan, Shen among them — into a room in his Kunming house and detained them, Lu Han declared for the Communists with some forty thousand troops, and Yunnan passed to Communist control without a battle for the city. The scene that opens this chapter's final section is corroborated in outline by later accounts.

One of the chapter's clearest self-exculpations. Writing as a pardoned war criminal for a 1960s historical-materials series, Shen repeatedly explains why he let assassination chances slip — fear of being caught, a losing cause, his mother's reproach. The reluctance is his own telling; the orders, the preparations, and his standing as Yunnan station chief are not in doubt, and the reader should weigh the motive he supplies against the acts he admits.
Tuo-cha (沱茶) is Yunnan's compressed bowl-shaped tea; the 'tuo-tea king' is a great tea merchant, a marker of the province's commercial wealth.
The gold-yuan note (金圆券), the currency the Nationalist government forced into use in 1948; by 1949 hyperinflation had rendered it worthless, which is why Yunnanese fell back on hard coin.
The half-open (半开) was Yunnan's provincial silver half-yuan coin. That people preferred it to the national gold-yuan note is a measure of how far the Nationalist currency had collapsed.

The Revolutionary Committee of the Chinese Kuomintang (民革), formed in Hong Kong in 1948 by Nationalists opposed to Chiang, which aligned with the Communists; its Yunnan people were secret-service targets.

ch14.anchor: the other side of the mountains
ch14.note: The other side of the mountains (山那边) was the local euphemism for the Communist-held liberated areas.

A pun on the division commander's name. Shi Butian means 'Stone Mends Heaven'; he jokes he should be Shi Bulu, 'Stone Mends Road,' since he cannot even keep the one railway repaired, let alone mend heaven.
Wuhuashan (五华山), the low hill in central Kunming that held the provincial government offices; the detained commanders were moved there during the uprising.

ch14.anchor: the charge against me is groundless
ch14.note: An allusion to mo-xu-you (莫须有), 'perhaps there is' — the phrase with which the Song minister Qin Hui is said to have justified the framing of the general Yue Fei, ever since a byword for a trumped-up charge. The imprisoned assemblyman's line turns it against his jailers.
The Chengdu-Chongqing railway (成渝铁路), promised to Sichuan for decades but left unbuilt under the Nationalists; it was completed only in 1952, under the People's Republic.
The Paoge (袍哥, 'gowned brothers'), the dominant secret-society brotherhood of Sichuan and Chongqing, whose bosses could turn out crowds and muscle at will.

ch15.note: The Yunnan July 15th Movement (云南七一五运动), part of the 1948 anti-US-support-Japan movement, culminating in the siege of Huize Hall at Yunnan University. Corroborated by Wikipedia and Yunnan University's own history — which put the arrests at close to a thousand and the detention at roughly half a year, well above Shen's 'over three hundred' and 'more than three months.' Writing as a perpetrator, he undercounts the scale of what he helped carry out.

The self-criticism register that frames the chapter. Shen wrote this in the 1960s as a pardoned war criminal for the CPPCC's historical-materials series; the confession of being 'one of the chief authors and perpetrators' and the profession of remorse are both genuine to that setting and shaped by it, and are worth reading as evidence of the conditions of the writing as much as of the man.

ch15.anchor: He Shaozhou told me how things stood
ch15.note: He Shaozhou (1902-1980), a Nationalist general and a nephew of He Yingqin, was commander-in-chief of the Yunnan Garrison Headquarters and the driving force of this crackdown. In the previous chapter he has already been removed from Yunnan by 1949; here, in 1948, he is at the height of his power.

ch15.anchor: taking the firewood from under the cauldron
ch15.note: Taking the firewood from under the cauldron (釜底抽薪): to solve a problem by removing its root cause rather than its symptoms — here, arresting the presumed Communist organizers rather than confronting the mass of students.

An allusion to two figures of the Three Kingdoms: Zhang Fei, the loud and impetuous warrior, and Zhuge Liang, the quiet master strategist. Shen's instruction is to ignore the noisy demonstrators and hunt the calm organizers who, he assumes, direct them.

ch15.anchor: more than thirty thousand strong in a great march against American support of Japan
ch15.note: The anti-US-support-Japan movement (反美扶日运动) of 1948, against Washington's policy of rebuilding Japan and its aid to Chiang's government. The Kunming march is documented on 17 June 1948, when the students went to the American consulate and delivered a protest addressed to President Truman, and some two dozen were arrested that night — corroborated. Documented accounts number the marchers at nearly ten thousand; Shen's 'more than thirty thousand' is inflated.

The Special Joint Conference (特种会报) was the Nationalists' standing inter-agency body for coordinating secret-service, party, government and military action against 'the Communists' and popular movements — the machinery through which the civil authorities were pulled into the armed suppression here.

Huize Hall (会泽院), the main building of Yunnan University. The students' stand there is remembered as the 'Defence of Huize Hall' (会泽院守卫战); the account in this chapter is the same episode told from the side of the men besieging it.

Xiong Qinglai (1893-1969), the eminent mathematician and president of Yunnan University from 1937 to 1949, who as a young professor had discovered and mentored the self-taught Hua Luogeng. His appearance to plead for the besieged students is a notable cameo.

An echo of the closing cry of Lu Xun's Diary of a Madman (1918), 'save the children,' by then a fixed phrase of protest against a devouring old order — here turned against the government firing on its own students.

ch15.anchor: plays the good man and leaves us to be the villains
ch15.note: He Shaozhou's complaint captures the division of labour Shen returns to elsewhere: Lu Han, the Yunnanese chairman, holds back and plays the protector, while the Centre's men do the killing. The same instinct to stall — and to spare — is what, a year later, has Lu Han release the September 9 detainees and defect to the Communists (see the previous chapter).

ch16.anchor: held that it was the work of Juntong agents
ch16.note: This chapter is Shen's fullest account of the Li Gongpu / Wen Yiduo killings (see the note in the Yunnan-liberation chapter). Both his telling and the mainstream record place the deed with the Yunnan Garrison Headquarters' special-agent battalion, acting on the order of its commander-in-chief Huo Kuizhang, who was cashiered for it. (Some public accounts name the Bureau's Kunming station instead; the garrison's secret-service units were part of the same Juntong / Bureau apparatus, so the two attributions are not cleanly separable.) What is distinctive here — the plot to plant false confessors implicating the Communists, and the claim that even the two men publicly shot were impersonated — is Shen's insider testimony and is not independently corroborated.
Killing with a borrowed knife (借刀杀人): to destroy an enemy by another's hand, keeping one's own clean — the thirty-sixth-stratagem name for making a third party do the damage.

ch16.anchor: beating the grass and startling the snake
ch16.note: Beating the grass and startling the snake (打草惊蛇): a careless move that alerts the quarry — here, an assassination so clumsy that it exposed the very hand it was meant to hide.

ch16.anchor: Long San, the third son of the former Yunnan chairman Long Yun
ch16.note: The attempt to pin the killings on Long Yun's son was aimed at Yunnan's displaced local faction. Long Yun, the province's old ruler, had been ousted by Chiang in 1945 (see the Yunnan-liberation chapter); framing his family would have let Huo strike the local power he distrusted while deflecting blame from his own men.

ch16.anchor: these two men proclaimed as shot were also impersonated by others
ch16.note: The chapter's most startling claim: the two 'assassins' executed before the public to close the case were themselves stand-ins — death-row prisoners got drunk and shot in their place — while the real killers were spirited to Dali and kept safe. It is Shen's word, from inside the operation, and cannot be checked against an outside record; but the double substitution is of a piece with the false-confessor scheme he helped set up earlier in the chapter.

ch16.anchor: an important pillar of the Chen Cheng clique
ch16.note: The Chen Cheng clique (the 'Earth-and-Wood faction', 土木系) was one of the Nationalist army's main factions, built around Chen Cheng's Eighteenth Army and Eleventh Division. Huo's membership is what let him read Chiang's mind through Chen Cheng — and what he wrongly bet would be rewarded.

ch16.anchor: it would not be a fault but a merit
ch16.note: Huo Kuizhang's remark, quoted without visible dissent, shows an unrepentance the memoir elsewhere performs remorse against: his regret is only that he killed the democrats a little too early to be thanked for it. Set beside Shen's own opening profession of shame, it marks how much the book's contrition is a matter of timing and audience.
